title: URL Shortener
oneLine: Create a compact alias, store the mapping durably, make redirects cache-heavy and fast, and push analytics and abuse checks off the critical path.
opening: I would separate the create path from the redirect path because reads dominate and have stricter latency. Creation validates and normalizes the URL, checks quotas and malicious content, chooses either a user alias or a generated 64-bit ID encoded in Base62, and stores an immutable mapping with owner, expiry, and status. Redirect first checks an edge/cache layer, then the partitioned mapping store, and emits analytics asynchronously. I would use 302 when accurate click analytics and destination changes matter, or 301 when permanent client/CDN caching is preferred. The mapping is sharded by short code, hot entries are cached, aliases are reserved atomically, and expiry/deletion uses tombstones so old links are not immediately reused.
ask: Are links editable, expiring, private, or one-time?
Do we need exact analytics and should bots be counted?
What is the read/write ratio, retention, and acceptable redirect latency?
scale: For 100M new links/day, average writes are about 1.2K/s; redirects may be 10–100× higher.
A 7-character Base62 space is about 3.5 trillion combinations; choose length from lifetime and safety margin.
Cache the hot working set and negative lookups briefly, but do not let negative caching block a just-created alias.

decisions.default: Generate a unique numeric ID then Base62-encode it.
decisions.why: It is collision-free and easy to partition; the ID service can allocate locally at scale.
decisions.switch: Use secure random aliases when enumeration or volume leakage is unacceptable; handle rare collisions with conditional insert.

decisions.default: 302 for editable links and server-side analytics; 301 for truly permanent high-cache redirects.
decisions.why: Browsers/CDNs may bypass the service after caching a 301.
decisions.switch: Use 307/308 when preserving HTTP method is relevant, though most short links are GET redirects.

decisions.default: A partitioned key-value/relational mapping keyed by short code, with durable replicas.
decisions.why: The dominant access pattern is a point lookup by alias.
decisions.switch: Use relational constraints when ownership, billing, alias reservation, and administrative queries dominate at moderate scale.

decisions.default: Emit an event asynchronously and aggregate later.
decisions.why: A click-tracking outage must not prevent redirection.
decisions.switch: Synchronous checks only for security policies that must block the redirect.

deepDives.title: Alias lifecycle
points: Reserve custom aliases with a unique conditional write.
Keep tombstones after expiry/deletion to prevent unsafe immediate reuse and stale-cache misrouting.
Version cache entries when destinations can be edited.

deepDives.title: Abuse and safety
points: Rate-limit creation and suspicious redirect traffic.
Scan destinations, use allow/deny reputation feeds, and support emergency takedown.
Prevent open-redirect header injection and normalize schemes/Unicode hostnames.

deepDives.title: Hot links
points: CDN/edge cache the mapping and redirect response where policy permits.
Replicate a single hot mapping rather than repartitioning the full store.
Sample analytics or aggregate at the edge to avoid an event storm.

failures.response: Conditional insert/unique constraint; retry with a new ID or return conflict for custom alias.

failures.risk: Cache serves an old edited destination
failures.response: Versioned invalidation, short TTL for editable links, and cache purge on change.
Buffered durable event log, sampling/backpressure, and never block redirect.
Asynchronous and synchronous safety tiers, takedown status in mapping, reputation checks, audit, and creation quotas.

questions.q: How do you prevent users from guessing other links?
questions.a: Use random or encrypted public aliases rather than sequential Base62 IDs, or accept enumeration for public links and protect private links with authorization/unguessable tokens.
Store expiry with the mapping, enforce it on redirect, and clean up asynchronously. A tombstone prevents stale caches or immediate alias reuse from resolving to the wrong destination.
By a stable hash of the short code. The redirect key is known, so point routing is straightforward. Keep ownership/admin indexes separately if needed.

questions.q: How do you count unique visitors?
questions.a: Emit raw events then approximate uniques with HyperLogLog or privacy-aware aggregation. Exact user identity requires authentication and changes the privacy model.

mistakes: Using a hash substring without a collision plan
seniorSignal: Treat redirect availability as more important than analytics. Explain lifecycle, abuse controls, cache invalidation, public-ID leakage, and how hot links are isolated.
implementation: Spring Boot API; PostgreSQL unique alias reservation or DynamoDB conditional writes
Snowflake/UUIDv7 + Base62 or cryptographically random token
Kafka click stream with separate aggregation and bot filtering
